<meta>This page continues a bibliographic survey of the works of Leone Abravanel (Leone Ebreo), specifically focusing on the publication history and various translations of his "Dialogues of Love" (Dialoghi d'amore).</meta>

A first Spanish translation was produced by Gedaliah ibn Yahya <note>original: "Guedella Yahia"</note> in Venice, 1568, in-quarto <term>in-quarto: a book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves, or eight pages</term>.

A second translation in the same language is that of Garcilaso Inca de la Vega <note>The famous historian and son of a Spanish conquistador and an Inca noblewoman</note>, published in Madrid by Madrigal in 1590, in-quarto.

This same work is found printed in the *Writers of the Cabalistic Art* <note>original: "Scriptores artis Cabalisticæ"</note>, according to the Latin translation by Johannes Carolus Saracenus; it was originally written in Italian.

One of the first editions of the French translation by Du Parc, Champenois <note>Denis Sauvage, a Renaissance translator and historiographer</note> is the Paris edition of 1551, in-duodecimo <term>in-duodecimo: a small book size where each sheet is folded into twelve leaves</term> — also Lyon, Rouillé, 1551, 2 volumes in 1, in-octavo <term>in-octavo: a common book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves</term>, and 1559, in-sixdecimo <term>in-sixdecimo: a very small "pocket" size book with sixteen leaves per sheet</term>, consisting of 820 pages excluding the index tables.

The first original edition of this work by Leone Abravanel <note>original: "Leone Abarbanel"</note> was printed in Rome by Antonio Blado in 1535, in-quarto, but is less sought after by collectors than the Aldine editions <note>Books produced by the famous Aldine Press in Venice, known for their high quality and anchor-and-dolphin logo</note> of 1541, 1545, 1549, 1552, and 1558, for example, in-octavo.

## tor, containing the principal

Withdraw, you shameless and beastly ones,
   Who, for the sake of animal appetite,
   And not for love, undertake your quests:
   Withdraw, you who are conquered by the Blind God. <note>original: "l’Aueugle" (the Blind One) — a common Renaissance reference to Cupid, the god of love, who was often depicted blindfolded to represent blind, unreasoning lust.</note>
But you, true humans, whose wills

   Read, read in this work of love,
   To better understand both beauty and goodness,

Then, realizing that which you lack,
   You will feel yourselves lifted on high,
   By a love that flies so straight and true,
Having left base passion behind on the earth,
   That it will set you exactly at the point
   Of unity, <note>In Neoplatonic philosophy, "Unity" refers to the "One," the highest state of being and the ultimate source of all beauty and goodness.</note> for your delight.

# THE CONTENT
## OF THE FIRST
### DIALOGUE.

-> * * * <-

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut initial 'L' depicting a squirrel climbing amidst grapevines and leaves within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

The first *Dialogue*, which is shorter than either of the other two, consists of only one part. At its beginning, the *Author*—writing under the name of *Philo* <note>The name Philo is derived from the Greek word for "lover."</note>—employs toward *Sophia* <note>Sophia is the Greek word for "wisdom." Together, the characters Philo and Sophia personify "Philosophy," the love of wisdom.</note> (whom he says he *loves* and *desires* because of the knowledge he has of her) several evasions, rhetorical traps <note>original: "captions" — a term for sophistical arguments intended to catch an opponent off guard</note>, and verbal maneuvers or arguments. These serve as inductions to lead into a truthful conversation and to arrive at the definition necessary before examining any subject one wishes to treat. Thus, to better discuss the essence of love and desire, he defines each separately; and in order to show the difference that might exist between them, he discourses upon the three kinds of

<meta>This page continues the summary of the first dialogue, picking up from the previous page's discussion of the three categories of "Good" (the Useful, the Delectable, and the Honest) which serve as the foundation for the philosophical inquiry into love.</meta>

Good, and first through the Useful, and then through the Delectable: under which he speaks of certain moral virtues and their opposites: speaking also of the conjunction of love and desire within the Delectable; of the cause of their diversity within these two Goods; which of the two—the Useful or the Delectable—is more extensive; and whether they may be found together in the same beloved object. Afterward, he speaks of love and desire toward the Honest <note>The "Honest" (Latin: *bonum honestum*) refers to that which is morally good or virtuous for its own sake, rather than for pleasure or utility.</note>: in what way it resembles the Delectable and the Useful; in what way and how it is different from them; and what the cause of this is. <margin>
The cause of the difference between love and desire in the **Useful** and the **Delectable**.
</margin>

**PHIL.** The cause is the difference in how one enjoys these two things, whether they are sought after or desired. Because the **Useful** exists in the continual possession of the thing, the more one possesses it, the more one enjoys its utility. For this reason, love does not arrive until one possesses the thing and desire ceases; and afterwards, love continues while one possesses it. If possession fails and truly ceases after one has had it, even though there may be desire, it will not be love. But as for the **Delectable**, its delight consists neither in possession, nor in habitation <note>habitation: here used in the sense of a settled or habitual state of having something.</note>, nor in perfect acquisition, but in a certain attention mixed with a lack <note>original: "defaut." The author argues that sensory pleasure requires a "lack" or "hunger" to be felt; without that "defect," the pleasure vanishes.</note>. A **Friend** is another self, to denote that whoever is in true friendship has a **double life**, constituted in two persons: that is to say, in his own, and in that of the **Friend**: in such a way that his friend is another self: and each of them embraces within himself two lives together: of which his own is one and that of the friend the other: and through an equal love, loves both persons: and likewise preserves both lives. <margin>Science</margin>

<margin>Wisdom</margin>
**Wisdom** is the habit of both of these together: that is to say, of the beginnings...

**PHILO.** Since God is the true and only Object of our **Happiness** <note>original: "Felicité"</note>, we love Him with both knowledge and love; but the Wise Men were of diverse opinions regarding these two acts, disputing whether the proper act of Happiness is to know God, or rather to love Him. <margin>Reasoning of those who hold that Happiness consists in loving God.</margin>

**PHILO.** Those who hold that Happiness consists in loving God bring forward this reason: namely, that Beatitude consists in the final act that our soul performs toward God, because He is the ultimate human End. He is also depicted shooting an arrow from his bow, because he strikes from afar and aims straight for the heart, as if it were his own target. Thus, the wound made by an arrow taken unawares—narrow at its entrance, deep in its penetration, not easily seen, difficult to care for, and very slow to heal—gives little sign to those who look only at the surface; but, regarding the interior, it is very perilous, and most often turns into an incurable fistula <note>In the medical language of the Renaissance, a fistula refers to a deep, narrow, and chronic ulcer or wound that is notoriously difficult to heal.</note>. Furthermore, just as the wound made by an arrow is not healed simply because the bow that shot it has been unstrung or broken, so the wound made by true love finds no remedy in any pleasure that **Fortune** <note>The personification of luck or worldly success.</note> might grant, or that the beloved might sometimes offer. Indeed, it cannot even be appeased by the loss of the beloved in irreparable death; so you must not be surprised if perfect love, being the son of **Reason**, is not governed by her.

This second Dialogue can be divided into three main parts. At the beginning of the first part, the author introduces **Sophia** <note>In these dialogues, Sophia (meaning "Wisdom" in Greek) acts as the student or seeker of knowledge.</note>, who reminds **Philo** <note>Philo (meaning "Love" or "Lover" in Greek) acts as the teacher, though his name also implies his longing for the wisdom Sophia represents.</note> of the promise he made her at the end of the first Dialogue: to tell her about the **genealogy** <note>The lineage or origin story; Philo intends to explain where the concept of Love comes from.</note> of Love. To do this more effectively, and as a preparation for the third Dialogue, Philo says it is necessary to first discuss Love's commonality, or rather its **universality** <note>original: "vniuersalité". The Neoplatonic idea that love is not just a human feeling, but a cosmic force found in all parts of the universe.</note>. He argues this because the common nature of Love is more obvious than its birth and lineage; and by starting with things that are manifest and known, one arrives at a knowledge of the unknown. Following this path, he speaks to her of the Love found in humans and in other animals, and of certain causes of love that are common to both. ### ON LOVE. DIALOGUE II. 141

<margin>Difference regarding the third cause of Love: beasts recognize a benefit better than non-virtuous men.</margin>

...temperament <term>complexion: the specific balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) that Renaissance thinkers believed determined a person’s personality and health</term>: just as hatred is also found among men without apparent cause, which hatred proceeds from a disproportionate difference in their temperaments. The Astrologers say that this amiable conformity comes from a similar and proportional arrangement of the Planets and celestial signs at the birth of both individuals; likewise, the hostile difference in their temperaments arises from a celestial position and arrangement that is dissimilar and disproportionate at their birth.

Thus we know this cause of love and friendship exists among men, but not at all among other animals. **SOPHIA.** What is the other cause? **PHILO.** The other comes from moral and intellectual virtues. These are the qualities through which excellent men are deeply loved by people of good character; the merits of these virtues create honorable love <note>original: "amour honneste"; a term for virtuous, selfless love, often contrasted with purely physical or selfish desire</note>, which is the most worthy of all. For human beings, for no other reason than virtue and wisdom, love one another effectively with a love that is more perfect and more firm than that which is based on the useful or the pleasurable <note>Philo is referencing Aristotle's three types of friendship: those based on utility, pleasure, or virtue</note>. It is for the sake of those two goods—the useful and the pleasurable—that all the other five causes of love are generated.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Sophia and Philo. The previous page established that honorable love is based on virtue and wisdom, distinguishing human relationships from those of animals. This page shifts the focus to whether non-living things can experience love.</meta>

->OF LOVE. DIALOGUE II.<-

This alone is honorable love <note>original: "amour honneste"; referring to virtuous, rational love</note>, and it is born of right reason; therefore, it is not found in irrational animals.

<margin>An argument against the idea that inanimate bodies possess love.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Very well, I have understood how many causes of love there are among men and concerning irrational animals. But I see that these are all specific to living beings, and not one of them applies to non-living bodies. Nevertheless, you say that love is common not only to animals, but also to other inanimate bodies; this seems strange to me. **PHILO.** Strange? Why?

<margin>A response to these arguments, in which he identifies three kinds of love.</margin>
**SOPHIA.** Because nothing can be loved unless it is first known, and inanimate bodies have no cognitive faculty <note>original: "vertu cognoscitiue"; the ability to perceive or know something</note> within them. Furthermore, love arises from the will and from appetite <term>appetition: a philosophical term for the natural drive or striving of a thing toward its own goal or "good"</term>, and it leaves an impression on the senses. Now, inanimate bodies have neither will, nor appetite, nor any sensation; how, then, can they have love?

She represents the celestial substance; Jupiter (who is the sovereign God, Creator of all things), being enamored of her, impregnated her with bodies that are shining in actuality: primarily the Sun and the Moon, to make her bring forth their light upon the terrestrial part of the world. However, Juno (who represents the globe of confused elements) did not consent to this; these shining bodies could not penetrate her with their rays, but were instead repelled from every part of the globe. <margin>Why he was nourished by Tethys.</margin>

### OF LOVE. DIALOGUE II.

# A summary of everything he has said in the present dialogue.

**SOPHIE.** Tell me how love gives life to the world, and how it makes a single thing out of so many other diverse ones.

**PHILO.** You will be able to easily understand it through the things already said. Sovereign God, through love, produces and governs the world, and assembles it into a single union: because, God being one alone in most simple unity, it is necessary that what proceeds from Him also be one in entire unity: for one proceeds from one, and from pure unity [comes] perfect union. Also, the spiritual world is unified with the corporeal world by means of love: and never would the separate intelligences <term>separate intelligences</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, these are non-physical, spiritual beings—often identified as angels—that guide the movements of the stars and planets.</note>, or divine Angels, unite with the celestial bodies, nor inform <note>To "inform" (French: "informer") is a philosophical term meaning to give shape, character, or life to matter.</note> them, nor provide them with life-giving souls, if they did not love them. Nor would intellectual souls ever unite with human bodies to make them rational, if love did not constrain them to it; nor would this soul of the world <term>soul of the world</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," a concept suggesting that the entire universe is a single living organism endowed with a soul.</note> unite with this globe of generation and corruption <note>This refers to the Earthly realm, where physical things are born ("generation") and eventually decay or die ("corruption").</note>, if it were not for love. Inferiors likewise unite with their superiors:

### 352
<header>OF COMM[UNICATION].</header>

I see you transforming into a Laurel <note>original: "Laurier". In Greek mythology, the nymph Daphne was transformed into a laurel tree to escape the pursuit of the god Apollo.</note>, so stationary in your place, and so unchanging in your purpose, and thus so difficult to be drawn toward my desire—even though at every hour I approach closer and closer to yours. And so you are always green and fragrant, like the Laurel: in whose fruit one finds no other flavor than bitterness and harshness, with a sharp juice for those who taste it. Thus, in my regard, you have become entirely a Laurel tree. And if you wish to see the sign of your transformation into a Laurel, take note that my silent harp would not sound at all, if it were not adorned with your most beautiful leaves. <note>Apollo, as the god of music, is traditionally depicted with a lyre or harp, and poets were crowned with laurel leaves to symbolize inspiration and victory.</note> SOPHIA. It would not be honorable for me, Philo, to confess that I loved you, nor would it be a courteous thing to deny it. Believe in what reason makes most suitable, even though you may fear the contrary. and, since the time now summons us to rest, it will be good for each of us to go and take it; then we shall see each other again shortly. Meanwhile, attend to your own refreshment: and remember your promise.

Secondly, an arriving quality changes the natural disposition of its subject; but light causes no change <note>original: "mutation."</note> in the transparent medium. Fourthly: when the source <note>original: "formateur," literally the "giver of form."</note> of such a quality is removed, some impression of it always remains in the subject for a time—just as one feels heat in water after it has been removed from the fire. But when the source of illumination is removed, nothing of the light remains in the transparent medium. Love in her. SOP. Of the soul for the intellectual.

Love of the soul for the corporeal.

**SOPHIA.** Tell me what it is, I pray you. **Philo.** Beauty has been defined in various ways; and it does not seem to me necessary now to declare all its definitions to you, nor to discern the true from the false: for that does not closely serve our purpose; and furthermore, I believe that, hereafter, it will be necessary for us to speak more amply of this Beauty. Thus, one of them (the love between the two parents) came to life at the start of the world's creation, and the other, the unitive love, at the completion of its formation. And as many times as the world might have been made, just as many times those two loves were then born.

<margin>The Ladder of Love to God.</margin>

In this manner, the **Arabs** <note>Referring to medieval Islamic philosophers like Avicenna (Ibn Sina) and Averroes (Ibn Rushd), whose works deeply influenced Renaissance thought</note> form a **circular line** of the universe: the beginning of this line is the **divinity of God**, and from there, succeeding by a chain from link to link, one arrives at **prime matter**, which is the point most distant from that Divinity. # OF GENESIS #

Adam awoke from his sleep; and then Adam said, "This time, this one is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be named **Woman** <term>Virago<gloss>A Latin term used in the Vulgate Bible to show the linguistic connection to *Vir* (man). Just as "woman" is derived from "man" in English, the author explains that her name reflects her origin from the male body.</gloss></term>, because she was taken from man." Then he continues, saying: "Therefore shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave unto his wife, and they shall be as one flesh."

<margin>The specific passage from which Plato took his concept of the division of the Androgyne.</margin>

Which is to say that, by being divided from one and the same individual, man and woman return to be reintegrated through marriage into one and the same carnal and individual being. And from this <note>The author is suggesting that the Greek philosopher Plato borrowed his ideas from the Hebrew scriptures.</note> comes Plato's division of the **Androgyne** into two halves (that is to say, male and female) and the birth of **Love**, which is the inclination remaining in each of the two halves to be reintegrated with its other part, and to be but one through the flesh. 

However, there is this difference between Moses and Plato: that Moses presents the division as being for the best (for he says, making God speak: *It is not good that man should be alone; let us make him a helper before him*) and, after the division, he recounts the first sin of Adam and Eve for having eaten from the forbidden tree of the knowledge of good and evil (for which sin a specific punishment was given to each of them). But Plato says that, before being divided, Man sinned, being...

**S O P H.** <note>Sophia, the personification of Wisdom.</note> This allegory, adapted to the Platonic myth of the Androgyne, pleases me as well; but I would like, Philo, for you to find a way to explain its application to our discussion on the birth of love.

<margin>The application of the allegorical meaning of the Androgyne to the birth of mutual love between the body and the intellect.</margin>

**P H I L.** <note>Philo, representing the lover of wisdom.</note> The application we shall make of this allegory for our discussion on the birth of love is this: all human loves and desires are born from the interrelated division of the human <term>intellect: the higher, rational part of the soul</term> and the human body. Because the intellect inclines toward its body (as the male to the female), it desires and loves the things belonging to it; and, if these are necessary and moderate, they are virtuous desires and loves, by virtue of their moderation and balance. However, if they are superfluous, these inclinations are lascivious and dishonest, and the acts are sinful.

<margin>That for the sake of the beautiful and of immortality, one desires to procreate, both physically and spiritually.</margin>
well-being. Now, their primary end <note>The "end" or *telos* refers to the ultimate goal or purpose of an action in Renaissance philosophy.</note> is the production of a Beauty similar to that which created the beauty and with which the mother is impregnated; and the final end is the desired immortality. For, as **Aristotle** says, since individual animals cannot be perpetual, they desire and strive to perpetuate themselves through the generation of their likeness; they often desire the life and being of this offspring more than their own, because it seems to them that their own lives are already passing away, and that their generated likeness is the part of them that is to be, and which makes their life immortal through continuous and similar succession.

These two ends also occur in the human soul; for, being pregnant with beauty, virtue, and intellectual **wisdom**, it always desires to procreate similar beauties through virtuous acts and wise <term>habits: ingrained dispositions or qualities of the mind</term>;

...parts to the whole, and the <term>commensuration</term> <note>The mathematical proportion or measurement of parts in relation to each other.</note> of the whole to these parts; and this is how many of those who have philosophized have defined it. Thus, beauty is proper to the measurable body and to the whole composed of its parts; and it properly presupposes <term>quantity</term> <note>The physical dimension, size, or volume of an object.</note> in a body. If beauty is attributed to <term>incorporeal things</term>, <note>Entities without physical form or substance, such as the soul, music, or mathematical concepts.</note> it is because they have parts in likeness to the body, of which parts they are composed proportionally by order (such as harmony, concordance, and well-ordered speech). For this reason, they are called beautiful by likeness to the composed and proportioned body. And so, regarding imaginative, rational, and mental considerations, the order of the parts to the whole is in likeness to the body, which is properly composed of commensurable parts called beautiful. It would therefore seem that the essence of beauty, like that of greatness, belongs to the body, which is the proper subject of quantity and the composition of parts.

Why well-proportioned bodies seem beautiful.

These parts are ordered intellectually <note>That is, according to a rational or divine design rather than by chance.</note> and are well-disposed toward their own functions and ends, unifying the whole and its parts—whether they are <term>homogeneous</term> (meaning they are similar throughout) or <term>heterogeneous</term> (meaning they are composed of diverse parts)—into the best form possible, so that the whole may be perfectly shaped and unified; and thus it becomes beautiful. But when matter is "disobedient" <note>Matter was often described as "rebellious" or "disobedient" in Renaissance philosophy because its chaotic nature resisted the perfect order of the spiritual form.</note>, the form cannot unify and order the parts intellectually to the whole in this way. —wn, a representation of it. Thus therefore, our soul has two faces, as I have told you regarding the Moon’s relation to the Sun and to the earth, of which one is toward the intellect, its superior, and the other toward the body, which is inferior to it.

<margin>

The first face, directed toward the intellect, is **intellectual reason** <note>The faculty of the soul that deals with abstract, universal truths rather than specific physical objects.</note>, by which our soul discourses with universal and spiritual **knowledge** <note>original: "cognition"</note>, extracting the intellectual forms and essences from particular and sensible bodies, always converting the corporeal world into the intellectual.

Here, the materiality of the known corporeal things is joined and mixed, and thus these two faces have contrary—or rather, opposite—movements. And just as our soul makes the corporeal into something incorporeal through its first face (or reasonable knowledge), so it draws the incorporeal toward the corporeal through its second face (or sensible knowledge), halting at the sensed bodies and mixing with them. <margin>How it should be understood that good effects come from good causes.</margin>
Even though the good effect comes from the good cause, this is not to say that the goodness and perfection of the effect matches that of the cause. Though the effect resembles its cause, it is not equal to it in perfective matters <note>perfective matters: things relating to the state of being complete or achieving their final, ideal form</note>. ->### ON THE GENEA[LOGY OF LOVE] ###<-

& and Ideal Intellect: so that, while it is granted that God, as the Wise or Intelligent Being, precedes sovereign Wisdom <term>Sapience: from the Latin 'sapientia,' referring to a higher, divine form of wisdom that is both knowledge and being</term> and intellect, it is not therefore to be granted that His own beauty precedes the Beauty of His sovereign wisdom; this is because wisdom is His very Beauty. As for Him, as the author of Wisdom, He is neither Beauty nor Wisdom, but the fountain from which flows the first Beauty and sovereign Wisdom; which, when it is communicated, makes the entire universe beautiful, along with all its parts. 

And thus there are three degrees of Beauty: namely, the Author of it, the **Beautifying Beautiful** <term>Beau bellifiant: the active, divine source that imparts beauty to others</term>; Beauty itself; and the participant in it, being the **Beautified Beautiful** <term>Beau bellifié: the created world which receives or "participates" in divine beauty</term>. Thus, the **Beautifying Beautiful**, the father of Beauty, is the sovereign God; Beauty itself is sovereign Wisdom and the First Ideal Intellect; and the **Beautified Beautiful**, the son of that Beauty, is the produced Universe. 

**SOPHIE.** The sublime abstraction of this second path of resolution so elevates my Intellect that I can hardly feel it is my own; rather, it seems to me a ray of that first divine Intellect.

<margin>
Of two Divine Loves toward the universe, further, to better find the end of universal love.

Since the first divine love is this state of being enamored <note>original: "enamourement"</note> of the sovereign God with His own sovereign beauty and wisdom, it was the productive cause of the universe in its likeness, along with its continual conservation; because the love, which first produced it, through its indissolubility, by always producing, conserves it. 

The second divine love, which is toward the produced universe, is that which carries the product to its final perfection; for, just as the first being of the universe comes from this first love which precedes it, so the final perfect Being of it proceeds from and is caused by the second divine love. This is the love that God has toward the universe, it having been already produced in the likeness of the Father; for loving Himself first, He desired to engender His likeness in beauty, and by this love preceding the son <note>original: "le fils" — a Neoplatonic metaphor where the created universe is viewed as the "son" or offspring of the Divine Creator</note>, He engendered him; and

Philo is explaining that a circle has two halves: one that moves away from the starting point to the furthest extreme, and another that returns from that extreme back to the beginning. <margin>Response</margin>
**PHILO.** I do not wish to remain in this debt for such a small remainder. <margin>Argument.</margin> Sensual delight is truly a passion in the sensitive soul <note>The "sensitive soul" refers to the part of the soul shared by humans and animals, which governs the five senses and physical emotions.</note>, just as sensual love is also a passion in that same soul—except that love is the first of its passions, and delight is the last, the end <note>original: "fin"; meaning the goal or final purpose</note> of that love. <image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicting two small figures positioned within the scrollwork of the letter.</image-desc>

Your reasons, Lady Sophia <note>The name "Sophie" or "Sophia" represents Wisdom personified, acting as the intellectual foil to the lover, Philo, in these dialogues.</note>, demonstrate more subtlety in your understanding than truth in your opinion: because if we did not love what we desired, we would desire what we did not love, and consequently what we would hold in horror and hatred. And thus, you must concede to me that you hold in horror that which you desire: but it would be better to concede the latter <note>Meaning, to admit that love and desire are linked.</note>, to ensure that love and desire may be together. For if you concede that you hold in horror what you desire, it would be a great contradiction, and you would be mistaken in this way.

S O P H. I am not mistaken, Philo,
and I will not give you the advantage in

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue between Philo and Sophia regarding the nature of love and desire. On the previous page, Sophia argued that love and desire are distinct because desire implies a lack of the object, whereas love implies its possession. Philo countered with the example of marriage to show they can coexist. This page begins with Sophia's reaction to that example and Philo's categorization of the "Good."</meta>

although your example does much for your argument, it still seems as strange to me as the doubt about which we are disputing.

**PHILO.** I will speak to you of this more universally. You know that love tends toward things that are good, or esteemed as such: and because there are three kinds of **Good**, there are also three kinds of love: namely, toward the **Delectable**, toward the **Profitable**, and toward the **Honest** <note>original: "Delectable, Profitable, & l'Honneste." Philo is referencing the classical Aristotelian division of the "Three Goods": the pleasurable (*delectabile*), the useful (*utile*), and the morally virtuous (*honestum*).</note>: the latter two of these goods ought to be loved in every season, both before they are acquired and after. But the **Delectable** is never loved afterward: because all things that delight those of our senses which by their nature are subject to matter, when they are possessed, are more often abhorred than loved <note>Philo argues that physical pleasures often lead to satiety or "disgust" once the craving is satisfied, unlike virtue or utility.</note>.

You must therefore concede to me, for this reason, that such delectable things are loved before they are possessed, and likewise when they are desired: for otherwise they would never be loved, and being loved neither for the present nor for the future, they would be hated. Thus you would desire that which you held in hatred: which would be the very **contradiction** I described to you.

### ANNOTATIONS ON THE
->second Dialogue.<-

*Some other superstitions*. page 142. line 21. I suspect that *superfluities* <note>original: "superfluitez." The translator is suggesting a philological correction where the source text might have used the wrong word.</note> should be used instead of *superstitions*, or rather to understand it as certain excessive curiosities <note>In the 16th century, "curiosity" often referred to over-scrupulousness or superstitious habits rather than a simple desire for knowledge.</note>, such as in France, making a fuss if someone has said to you *it is not true* <note>original: "il n’est pas vray." ***Organized.*** <note>original: "Organise"</note> Composed of limbs and bodily instruments.

***Celestial Orbs.*** Circles and roundnesses of the heavens. <note>In pre-modern astronomy, these were the concentric spheres thought to carry the planets and stars around the Earth.</note>

## P

***Privation.*** The Philosophers use this word for the opposite of Being, which we explain in its [proper] place. <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality that a subject should naturally possess.</note>

***Thought.*** <note>original: "Pensée"</note> I use this word, most often, for what he [the author] calls "Mind" <note>original: "Mente", from the Latin "Mens"</note>: and it is used in French for understanding, and sometimes for the virtue of the soul, where the act of thinking takes place, and sometimes for the thinking itself.

***Piety.*** It is sometimes an office or duty toward God. Sometimes toward parents and friends, sometimes toward those of the same country; and finally toward the poor and suffering. Regarding God, [it is used] for graciousness or kindness.

***Participate.*** I use this both for taking a part and for giving it, as my Author also does.

***Potential.*** <note>original: "Puissance"</note> A thing is said to be "in potential" by the Philosophers when it is possible for it to become something that it is not yet; just as from a

I also use **potential** <note>original: "potentiel"</note> sometimes.

***Arctic & Antarctic Poles.*** They are two points or stars, one toward the South <note>original: "Midi"</note>, the other toward the North <note>original: "Septentrion"</note>, just as he describes them.

***Precisely.*** From a fixed point.

***To Penetrate.*** To pierce through, or simply to pierce: and likewise for its derivatives.

***Propagation.*** Extensive generation or production and begetting.

***Particles.*** Small parts.

***Passion.*** For our purposes, this is a disturbance, subjecting the spirit to suffer and endure fear and hope, through the desire for what is lacking: or, afterwards, to suffer joy or trouble. <note>In this period, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon (passivity) rather than just strong emotion.</note>

***To Pre-exist.*** To be beforehand: and likewise for its derivatives, such as **Pre-existence**, etc.

***Real.*** A thing is said to be real when it truly and in fact exists: and its adverb **Really** is to say truly and in effect: and likewise understand the words that descend from this **Real**, each... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing with "each one" on the following page.</note>

one in its place.

*Reason.* Our Author, most often, uses this word to signify that faculty of our understanding, which must judge things after the <term>reasoning</term> <note>original: "ratiocination"</note> or discourse conducted upon them, to know if they are good or bad, true or false, and so on.

*Relation.* Is a relationship made from one thing to another, such as from father to son, and from son to father, the one always presupposing the other: but, for the point I promised you on page 175, see our annotations on the second Dialogue.

*Religion.* A certain way of conducting oneself toward God.

### S

*Sapience.* Concerning Men, this word can be taken for wisdom, understanding, and knowledge of things divine and human; but concerning God, it is something higher still, as he demonstrates sufficiently in the final part of the 3rd Dialogue. You will understand similarly of **Sapient** <note>Wise, in a spiritual or elevated sense</note> and its derivatives. I did not wish to use the words Sage or wisdom: because they do not
